ta-l1d27q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 27 turns to the name 'Word' and announces three articles: whether 'Word' is properly in God; whether it is said essentially or only personally; and whether it implies a relation to creatures.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that 'Word' is not properly said of God. A name signifying a bodily operation fits God only metaphorically, and 'verbum' comes from the beating of the air (verberatio aeris), as Priscian says.
claims: Verbum derives from verberatio aeris.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e112.summary: Second argument. Among our things a word seems most transient and is not subsistent, while whatever is said of God is permanent and subsistent.
claims: Words are transient.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e115.summary: Third argument, against the reply that God has a word of the heart, not of the voice. Anselm says for the highest spirit to speak is to behold by thinking (cogitando), and thinking does not fit God, since cogitatio is the discursus of a reason inquiring and proceeding from one thing to another.
claims: Speaking is beholding by thinking, which is discursive.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e119.summary: Fourth argument. The word of the heart is a conception of the intellect, which conceives only the intelligible species it forms. God knows not by a species but sees himself by his essence and so knows all things.
claims: God knows by essence, not by a formed species.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e122.summary: Sed contra from John 1:1: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.'
claims: Scripture calls the Son the Word.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e128.summary: Second sed contra. Augustine says the Word is nothing but begotten wisdom, which is in God.
claims: Word is begotten wisdom.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e131.summary: Thomas's determination. God is undoubtedly a Word and properly called so. As the Gloss on John says, there is a threefold word in us: of the heart, of the voice, and the word having the image of the voice. This is needed because speech is a bodily operation requiring what every deliberate bodily motion requires: deliberation and judgement in the intellect; a particular power apprehending the particular intention, since intellect is of universals and operations of singulars (De anima 3); and bodily motion through motive powers in muscles and nerves, like a syllogism with a universal major in the intellect, a particular minor in sense, and the operation as conclusion. Speech in the intellect alone is the word of the heart, also called the word of the thing as its immediate likeness, which Damascene calls the natural motion of the intellect, its light and splendour, and Augustine the word impressed on the soul. In the imagination, when one imagines the words to express the concept, it is the word having the image of the voice, Damascene's word spoken in the heart, Augustine's word thought in the bosom of the mind. In bodily action through the tongue it is the word of the voice, Damascene's messenger of understanding, Augustine's word pronounced with syllables. The word of the voice and the word with its image are said of God only metaphorically, but the word of the heart, which is in the intellect alone, is said of God more properly than of others. There are grades in the intellect's operations: first the simple gaze on the intelligible, which does not yet have the character of a word; second the ordering of the intelligible to manifestation, to another, as when one speaks to another, or to oneself, as when one speaks to oneself, and this first has the character of a word. So a word is an emanation from the intellect by way of manifesting. Since the gaze may be of the true simply or of the true extended to the good and fitting, which is perfect apprehension, there is a twofold word: of a thing uttered that pleases, which breathes love, the perfect word, and of a thing that displeases, so Augustine says a word is impressed on the mind even if the thing displeases.
claims: God is properly a Word, as word of the heart, more properly than creatures.
A word is an emanation from the intellect by way of manifestation, beyond the simple gaze.
The perfect word breathes love.
concepts: Damascene and Augustine on the word

ta-l1d27q2-d1e134.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although 'word' was imposed from bodily motion, the last stage of our speech, it was imposed to signify whatever is said outwardly or inwardly. So though the derivation of the name does not fit God, the thing signified does, as often happens, as with 'person'.
claims: The name's derivation need not fit God; its signification does.
concepts: id a quo vs. id ad quod nomen imponitur

ta-l1d27q2-d1e137.summary: Reply to the second argument. The word of the voice neither remains nor subsists in us, but the word of our heart remains, though it does not subsist. So, though a word does not by its concept remain or subsist, it has different grades of perfection in different subjects, and the divine Word is permanent and subsistent, as was said of love (Dist. 10).
claims: The divine Word is permanent and subsistent by the perfection of its subject.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e141.summary: Reply to the third argument. There is no thinking (cogitatio) properly in God, but Anselm used the name by likeness: as in thinking reason goes out from one thing to another by collecting, so the character of a word is completed in an emanation and going out from the intellect, which adds to simple intuition something like thinking.
claims: Anselm's 'cogitatio' is used by likeness to the word's emanation.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e144.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The divine intellect does not understand its essence by a species essentially or really different from the essence, but understands its essence by its essence, so the essence is as knower, as known, and as that by which it is known. As knower there is truly the character of intellect, as known the character of the understood, and as that by which it is understood the character of word.
claims: In God the essence functions as knower, known, and word (that by which it is understood).

ta-l1d27q2-d1e161.summary: First argument that 'Word' is not said personally. Augustine says the Word we mean to suggest is knowledge with love, and knowledge is said essentially.
claims: Word is knowledge with love.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e164.summary: Second argument. Whatever can be understood without the distinction of persons is essential, and without it one can still understand that the divine intellect manifests itself to itself and to creatures. Since 'word' adds to intellect only an order of manifestation, it is essential, like understanding.
claims: Self-manifestation is intelligible without distinction of persons.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e167.summary: Third argument. A word is the term of saying, and each person can say himself and his essence, so the essence is a word and each person is a word. Each does not say himself by the Father's Word, since saying by one's own word is more perfect, nor by a word proceeding from himself, which would make more than three persons, so by a word that is himself.
claims: Each person speaks himself by a word that is himself.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e170.summary: Fourth argument. A word is a conception of the intellect, which is only the intelligible species formed in it, so in God the word would be what functions as species, by which something is understood, the principle of understanding. If only the Son were the Word, he would be the principle of the Father's understanding, which Augustine rejected (Dist. 5).
claims: A personal Word would make the Son the Father's principle of understanding.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e174.summary: Sed contra. Augustine says he is called Word by the same as Son and as begotten wisdom, which are personal.
claims: Word, Son, and begotten wisdom go together.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e177.summary: Second sed contra. Augustine says though there are three who speak, there is only one Word.
claims: Three speakers, one Word.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e180.summary: Third sed contra. 'Word' implies an order of going out, a conception of the intellect, and is said relatively (as the text says), all of which pertain to the persons.
claims: Word implies procession and relation.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e189.summary: A further question: if 'Word' is said personally, is only the Son the Word? First argument against: as the Son goes out from the Father manifesting him, so does the Spirit, so the character of word fits both.
claims: The Spirit also manifests the Father.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e192.summary: Second argument. Intellect is a medium between nature, which it follows, and will, which it precedes, and a medium belongs to both extremes, so the Son, proceeding by nature, is no more the Word than the Spirit, proceeding by will.
claims: Intellect lies between nature and will.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e195.summary: Third argument. A cause is manifested by its effect, and the divine intellect causes all creatures as an artisan's intellect causes artefacts, so all creatures can be called God's word.
claims: Creatures manifest the divine intellect.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e198.summary: Sed contra. Augustine says that as only the Son is called Word in the Trinity, only the Spirit is called Gift, so as Gift does not fit the Son, Word does not fit the Spirit.
claims: Only the Son is Word, as only the Spirit is Gift.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e207.summary: Thomas's determination on whether 'Word' is personal. Some say 'to say' is used three ways of God: as 'to understand', essential; as 'to beget', notional; and as 'to create', essential with a connotation of creatures, and only the second has a corresponding word, so 'Word' is only personal. This seems false, since nothing is said without a word, so as often as 'say' is used, 'word' must be too. Others say 'to say' in general is to manifest one's intellect, to another as by a vocal word, or to oneself as by a word of the heart, and God does both, creating the creature as a quasi-vocal word and begetting the Son as he manifests himself to himself, the word of the heart, so 'Word' is always personal. This also seems false: the word by which one speaks to oneself is only a conception of the intellect, either the operation of understanding or the understood species, the likeness of the thing; without one of these no one understands, since each is formally that by which one understands. So in this sense one understands only by the word of one's intellect, and if the only word in God were the personal Word, the Son, the Father would understand formally by the Son, rejected in Dist. 5. So, with others, 'word' by the force of the term can be taken personally and essentially. It does not signify only a relation, like 'Father' or 'Son', but something absolute together with a relation, like 'knowledge', though knowledge's relation is to what it is of, the knowable, while word's relation is of origin, to the speaker it is from. Such relations in God are either real, requiring real distinction (paternity and filiation, since nothing is father and son to the same), or only of reason, not requiring real distinction, like the implicit relation of operation to operator, which in God differ only conceptually. If the relation implied by 'word' is of reason only, nothing prevents its being said essentially, and this seems to suffice for the character of word as transferred from us to God, since in us the word is the understood species or perhaps the operation itself, neither really distinct from the divine essence. If it implies a real relation requiring distinction, it must be said personally, since the only real distinction in God is of persons, as with love (Dist. 18). Since a word is the likeness of the understood thing as conceived in the intellect and ordered to manifestation, this species can be taken as that by which something is formally understood in God, and so, since the essence is understood and manifested by itself, the essence will be the word, with word, intellect, and thing differing only conceptually; or as something really distinct from what it is the likeness of, and so 'word' is personal and fits the Son, in whom the Father is manifested as a principle in what proceeds from it by way of intellect. But in the usage of the saints and common speech 'word' implies a really distinguishing relation, as Augustine says the Word is begotten wisdom. So the question matters little, since it concerns not the thing but the signification of a word, which is conventional, where usage counts most: one should use names as the many do and judge of things as the wise do (the Philosopher), and when the things are settled, controversy over words is idle (Lombard, II, Dist. 14). Still, what is said of God should not be extended beyond the use of Sacred Scripture.
claims: 'Word' can be taken essentially (relation of reason) or personally (real relation of origin).
In usage 'Word' implies real distinction and is personal; the question concerns signification, governed by usage.
If only the personal Word existed, the Father would understand formally by the Son.
concepts: relations of reason vs. real relations
Father does not understand by the Son

ta-l1d27q2-d1e210.summary: Reply to the first argument. Knowledge does not give the whole character of word, since knowledge and wisdom are said as resting and remaining in their subject, and so only essentially, though they can be appropriated. A word says an emanation of the intellect going out to manifest itself, and since this going out can be understood as a really distinct thing, as the Son goes out from the Father, or only conceptually, as understanding is from the divine intellect, 'word' is said sometimes essentially and sometimes personally, like love.
claims: Word, unlike knowledge, implies emanation, which can be real or conceptual.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e213.summary: Reply to the second argument. Without the distinction of persons the divine intellect can still manifest itself to another, by creating or inspiring knowledge in a creature, and to itself, by turning back on what it understood to make clear whether it is true, which is properly speaking in the heart. But there would not be a manifestation of the principle in something really distinct, existing by way of intellect in the same nature.
claims: Without the persons there would be essential self-manifestation, but no real manifestation of a principle in another.
Each person speaks himself by the essential word.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e220.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. It must not be granted that the Father understands from the Son or in the Son as in an object or species by which he knows, since that would make the Son a principle of the Father. But the Father understands himself and others in the Son, inasmuch as he sees the Son to be his likeness and the likeness of all things, as a principle is seen in what it is principle of, though also in itself, as I can see a man in his image though I also see him directly. So the Father sees himself and all things in himself, yet can see them in the Son, as he can see himself in a creature that represents him imperfectly.
claims: The Father does not understand by the Son but can see himself and all things in the Son as his image.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e223.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. Augustine takes 'word' as implying real going out and distinction from the speaker, not as a distinction of reason suffices for the character of word, and so takes it only personally.
claims: Augustine's usage is personal.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e226.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. In God there is only one Word, yet there is a personal and an essential word, since the person is not distinct from the essence, so neither is excluded by an exclusive expression.
claims: One Word, both personal and essential, since person and essence are not distinct.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e229.summary: Reply to the third sed contra. All those features can be taken really or conceptually, and either suffices for the character of word, so it is said both essentially and personally.
claims: Procession and relation can be real or conceptual.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e239.summary: Thomas's determination on the further question. Taken personally, 'Word' fits only the Son, not the Spirit, since the Spirit proceeds by way of will and so is properly called Love and Gift, while proceeding by way of nature or intellect belongs to the Son, who is properly called both Begotten and Word.
claims: Personally, only the Son is Word, proceeding by nature and intellect.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e242.summary: Reply to the first argument. Being manifestative is not enough for a word, or every effect would be the word of its cause, which can be said only metaphorically; a procession of intellect must be understood, which does not fit the Spirit.
claims: A word requires procession of intellect, not just manifestation.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e245.summary: Reply to the second argument. The Spirit proceeds from two, so his procession is by way of the conformity of love, from the union of will in those who will, and so only by way of will. Both the procession of intellect and that of nature are from one alone, and not from one as united to another, if the agent is perfect as the divine agent is, so both modes of procession fit the person who is from one alone.
claims: Nature and intellect proceed from one; love from the union of two.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e248.summary: Reply to the third argument. A creature cannot properly be called a word but rather the voice of the word: as voice manifests a word, the creature manifests divine art. So the saints say God spoke every creature by one Word, and creatures are like voices expressing one divine Word, as Augustine says all things cry out 'God made us'; but this is said only metaphorically.
claims: Creatures are the voice of the Word, metaphorically.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e264.summary: First argument that 'Word' always implies a relation to creatures. Augustine glosses 'he spoke and they were made' as 'he begot the Word in whom it was that creatures be made'.
claims: The Word contains the making of creatures.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e270.summary: Second argument. Augustine says the Word is the Father's operative power, which is said with respect to creatures.
claims: Word as operative power.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e273.summary: Third argument. Anselm says God by speaking himself spoke every creature, and by speaking he begot the Word equal to himself, so the Word implies a relation to creatures, which are spoken by it.
claims: Speaking himself, God spoke creatures.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e277.summary: Fourth argument. An artisan knows artefacts only by turning to the art-form in him, so turning to the art and to the artefacts is the same. The Word is the art of everything the supreme artisan made, so the Father's intellect turns to the artefacts only by turning to the Word, and conversely.
claims: The Word is the divine art.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e280.summary: Sed contra. Nothing implying relation to creatures belongs to God from eternity, like 'Lord', but 'Word' does ('In the beginning was the Word').
claims: Relations to creatures are temporal.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e286.summary: Second sed contra. Every name connoting an effect in creatures signifies the divine essence, and 'Word' is personal, at least sometimes.
claims: Names connoting effects are essential.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e289.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Word' is said sometimes with and sometimes without relation to creatures. Whether said personally or essentially, a word is a conceived species containing the likeness of what is said, and of the speaker when one speaks oneself. The divine essence, or the Father, pre-contains the likeness of every creature as exemplar, so what is signified as the species or likeness of the Father or the essence, if it is a perfect likeness, contains the likeness of all things. But turning to a species need not always be turning to what it is the likeness of, since one can turn to a species or image as the species of the thing, which is the same turning as to the thing, or as a thing in itself, as one considers a statue as stone or as a likeness of Socrates or Plato. Since God is the likeness and species of all things, his intellect can turn to him absolutely, as a thing, or as the likeness of all things, and he knows himself both ways, though by one operation. So if 'word' follows the divine intellect's gaze on itself absolutely, it is said without relation to creatures, essentially or personally; if it follows the intellect turning to itself as the likeness and exemplar of all things, it includes a relation to creatures, as of art to artefacts, and so the name 'art' properly fits the Word. If 'word' is taken by the order of manifestation to another, it always implies a relation to creatures, since such manifestation of the divine intellect is by producing creatures.
claims: 'Word' implies relation to creatures only as the exemplar or as manifestation to another, not absolutely.
An image can be considered as a thing or as a likeness of something else.
concepts: image as thing vs. as likeness

ta-l1d27q2-d1e292.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although in the Word is that from which every creature is made, consideration of the Word and of him whose Word it is does not depend on considering creatures, so 'Word' does not necessarily imply relation to creatures.
claims: The Word can be considered without creatures.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e295.summary: Reply to the second argument. The Word is called the Father's operative power by way of art, and as signified as art it is signified with respect to creatures, but not necessarily when signified as word. Compare the Holy Spirit: he is the love by which the Father loves the Son, which is the reason for his love for creatures, which he draws to the likeness of his love; as love absolutely he is named 'Love' with no connotation of creatures, but as the reason of what is freely given to creatures he is named 'Gift', which implies relation to creatures. So with 'Word' and 'art': 'Word' can be said absolutely, but 'art' implies relation to artefacts.
claims: 'Art' implies relation to creatures; 'Word' need not, as 'Gift' does and 'Love' need not.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e299.summary: Reply to the third argument. By one and the same Word the Father spoke himself and every creature, but the consideration differs as he is spoken and creatures are. He has absolute knowledge of himself, absolute knowledge of creatures, and comparative knowledge, as knowing himself their cause, which differ only conceptually. So the Word as that by which the Father speaks himself does not require relation to creatures, but as that by which he speaks creatures it does, so the Word is understood both absolutely and with relation to creatures.
claims: One Word speaks Father and creatures, under conceptually distinct considerations.
concepts: one Word for self and creatures

ta-l1d27q2-d1e302.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. An artisan can turn to the art-form in him three ways: as the likeness of the thing to be made, turning simply to the artefact without considering his art; to the form as having being in his soul, considering it absolutely as a thing, with no thought of the artefact; or comparing the two, considering the form as the cause of what he makes. So too the divine intellect turning on itself, as a thing, as the likeness of things, or as the likeness that causes what it assimilates to itself, though in God these cognitions are simultaneous and not really different.
claims: The art-form can be considered as likeness, as thing, or as cause.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e305.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. 'Word' implies relation to creatures not in act but as in habit, like 'Gift', so both are eternal.
claims: Word and Gift relate to creatures habitually, so are eternal.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e308.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. Every effect in creatures is common to the whole Trinity, so whatever implies relation to creatures leads to knowledge of the essence, as a cause is known in its effect. But since not only the essence is ordered to creatures but also personal procession, which is the reason for the procession of creatures, something personal can be signified with relation to creatures, and such a name of principle signifies the person principally and leads consequently to understanding the essence, as with 'Word' and 'Gift'.
claims: Personal procession is the reason of creation, so personal names can connote creatures.

ta-l1d27q2-d1e318.summary: An expositio textus. 'If the divine nature is the Father, it begot the Son' does not follow: though Father and generation are really the same, the verb 'generate' signifies the property as inhering in and determining its subject, and since the essence is not determined by the property as a subsistent, the essence is not said to beget; 'Father' signifies the same property as subsistent, so by real identity the essence is said to be the Father. 'They differ from each other': difference is not properly in God, since it opposes likeness as diversity opposes unity, but here it is taken broadly for distinction.
claims: 'The essence is the Father' is true, but 'the essence begets' is not.
'Difference' is used broadly for distinction.

ta-l1d27q2-Dd1e156.summary: The first quaestiuncula of Article 2 gives arguments that 'Word' is said essentially (knowledge with love, self-manifestation without persons, each person speaking himself) and contrary arguments from Augustine that it is personal.

ta-l1d27q2-Dd1e184.summary: The second quaestiuncula of Article 2 asks whether, if 'Word' is personal, only the Son is the Word, with arguments that the Spirit and creatures also manifest, and Augustine's parallel between Word and Gift.

ta-l1d27q2-Dd1e202.summary: Thomas's solution to the first quaestiuncula rejects both the view that 'Word' is only personal and the view that it is always personal, since the Father would then understand formally by the Son. 'Word' signifies something absolute with a relation of origin, which can be of reason (essential word) or real (personal Word). In common and patristic usage it is personal, and the question concerns signification, governed by usage within the limits of Scripture. The Father does not understand by the Son but can see himself and all things in the Son as his image.
claims: 'Word' can be essential or personal; usage makes it personal.
The Father does not understand formally by the Son.

ta-l1d27q2-Dd1e234.summary: Thomas's solution to the second quaestiuncula holds that, taken personally, only the Son is the Word, since procession by intellect and by nature are from one alone, while the Spirit proceeds by will from two. Manifestation alone does not make a word, and creatures are only metaphorically the voice of the Word.
claims: Only the Son is the personal Word.

ta-l1d27q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces three articles on 'Word': whether it is properly in God, whether it is essential or personal, and whether it implies relation to creatures.

ta-l1d27q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 holds that God is properly a Word. Distinguishing the word of the heart, the word with the image of the voice, and the word of the voice, Thomas says only the first, in the intellect alone, is said properly of God, and more properly than of creatures. A word is an emanation from the intellect ordered to manifestation, beyond simple intuition, and the perfect word breathes love. The name's bodily derivation does not matter, the divine Word is subsistent by the perfection of its subject, Anselm's 'thinking' is analogical, and in God the essence is knower, known, and word.
claims: God is properly a Word, as word of the heart.
A word is an intellectual emanation ordered to manifestation.

ta-l1d27q2-Dd1e148.summary: Article 2, in two quaestiunculae, asks whether 'Word' is said essentially or personally and whether only the Son is the Word. Thomas holds that 'Word' signifies something absolute with a relation of origin. It can be essential, where the relation is of reason, or personal, where it is real. Usage makes it personal, and the Father does not understand by the Son. Taken personally, it belongs only to the Son, who proceeds from one by intellect and nature, while the Spirit proceeds by will from two. Creatures are only metaphorically the voice of the Word.
claims: 'Word' is essential or personal according to the relation implied; usage makes it personal.
Only the Son is the personal Word.

ta-l1d27q2-Dd1e256.summary: Article 3 holds that 'Word' implies relation to creatures not always but only as the exemplar of things (as art) or as manifestation to another (by creation). Taken absolutely, as the divine intellect's gaze on itself, it implies none. An image can be considered as a thing or as a likeness. One Word speaks the Father and creatures under conceptually distinct considerations. Word, like Gift, relates to creatures habitually and so eternally, and personal procession, as the reason of creation, allows personal names to connote creatures.
claims: 'Word' implies relation to creatures only as exemplar or manifestation to another.
Personal names can connote creatures because personal procession is the reason of creation.

ta-l1d27q2-Dd1e313.summary: The Expositio textus explains why 'the essence is the Father' is true but 'the essence begets' is not, and that 'difference' is used broadly for distinction.
claims: The essence is the Father but does not beget.

ta-l1d27q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 27 treats the name 'Word'. Article 1 holds that God is properly a Word, as the word of the heart, an emanation from the intellect ordered to manifestation. Article 2 holds that 'Word' signifies something absolute with a relation of origin and so can be taken essentially, with a relation of reason, or personally, with a real relation. Usage makes it personal, and so taken it belongs only to the Son, who proceeds by intellect from one. Article 3 holds that 'Word' implies relation to creatures only as exemplar or as manifestation to another, not absolutely.
claims: God is properly a Word.
'Word' can be essential or personal; personally it is the Son alone.
'Word' connotes creatures only as exemplar or manifestation ad extra.
